name: Lutein and zeaxanthin supplements

card.summary: Plant carotenoids sold for eye health; the research is about macular degeneration, not cosmetic eye brightness, and its overall result there is modest.
card.aka: Lutein, zeaxanthin, macular pigment supplements, marigold extract
card.note: Studied for age-related macular degeneration, not for cosmetic eye appearance; excess intake can cause harmless skin yellowing (carotenodermia).

quick.overview:
Lutein and zeaxanthin are yellow plant pigments (xanthophyll carotenoids) found in leafy greens and egg yolks. They concentrate in the macula, the central part of the retina, and are sold as over-the-counter supplements marketed for eye health.

Most research concerns age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and cataract rather than how the eyes look. A large US trial (AREDS2) and a later Cochrane review are the main reference points; they report small or no overall effects on AMD progression.
quick.mechanism: The pigments accumulate in the macula, where they are thought to filter blue light and act as antioxidants, although their exact functional role there is described as not fully established. Supplement studies often measure macular pigment density or visual function.
quick.risks: Excess intake of carotenoids is associated with a harmless yellow-orange skin tint (carotenodermia). Lutein is sold as a dietary supplement in the US and approved as a food additive (E161b) in the EU. Supplements are not a studied treatment for eye whiteness or brightness.

lead: Lutein and zeaxanthin are xanthophyll carotenoids, yellow plant pigments that people obtain from foods such as leafy greens, egg yolks and orange peppers. They are isomers the body can interconvert, and they accumulate in the macula, the central part of the retina [1][22]. Supplements combining the two, usually extracted from marigold petals, are sold mainly for eye health and make up the largest segment of the lutein market [1].

For appearance, they are taken with the aim of healthy, clear-looking eyes and, by some users, skin that is better protected from sun and blue light. Dietary carotenoids also tint skin: very high intake produces a yellow-orange warmth called carotenodermia, which some people notice as a golden tone [1]. A 2025 systematic review of 47 human studies found that carotenoid-based supplements were among the categories with the greatest photoprotection evidence, although it assessed carotenoids as a group rather than lutein alone [13].

Most clinical research concerns medical outcomes: age-related macular degeneration (AMD), cataract, macular pigment density and visual function [3][12]. The landmark Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 (AREDS2) enrolled 4,203 people with intermediate or advanced AMD from 2006 [3][21]. Adding lutein and zeaxanthin to the original antioxidant formula had no added overall effect on progression to advanced AMD, with a roughly 25 percent reduction reported in participants whose diets were low in these pigments, and a 2023 Cochrane review of 26 studies found little effect of the supplements alone on progression [1][21].
infobox: Leafy greens, egg yolk, paprika, marigold petal extract [1]
Lutein 10 mg + zeaxanthin 2 mg per daily dose, with vitamins C, E, zinc and copper [21]

paras: Lutein is made only by plants; animals obtain it through diet. It is abundant in kale and spinach and present in egg yolks. Zeaxanthin is its isomer and the two can be interconverted in the body [1]. Commercial supplements are commonly extracted from Mexican marigold petals [1].
Both pigments are found concentrated in the human macula, though encyclopedic sources note that their precise functional role there is not fully established [1].

Lutein is a red-orange crystalline pigment, one of about 600 known carotenoids, that dissolves in fats and not in water, which is why it is usually eaten with oils or egg yolk [1]. Per the USDA FoodData Central ranking cited by Wikipedia, dry paprika powder and frozen spinach have the highest levels [1].

Zeaxanthin takes its name from Zea mays (maize) and gives colour to paprika, corn, saffron and goji berries. Its three stereoisomers include the main natural (3R,3'R) form; the macula also holds meso-zeaxanthin, and a binding protein is thought to draw lutein and zeaxanthin into retinal tissue [22]. Leafy greens are rich in lutein but contain little zeaxanthin, while orange peppers, yellow cornmeal and spirulina are notable zeaxanthin sources [22].

The mainstream use is eye health: supplements combining lutein and zeaxanthin are taken in the hope of supporting the macular pigment, and reviews describe studies on age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, myopia and cataract.[12] For appearance, people take them with the aim of healthier-looking eyes and, in some cases, skin that is better protected from sun and blue light.

A 2025 systematic review of oral supplements and photoprotection included 47 human studies covering carotenoids, polyphenols, Polypodium leucotomos, vitamins, coenzyme Q, squalene and fatty acids, and reported that the greatest evidence of photoprotection was for polyphenol, carotenoid-based and Polypodium leucotomos supplementation.[13] Lutein was one of the carotenoids among the search terms; the review addresses carotenoid supplements as a group rather than lutein alone.[13]
Carotenoids in the diet can also color the skin: the yellow-orange tint of carotenodermia is the documented effect of very high intake, which some people may notice as a warmer skin tone.[1]

Lutein is made only by plants and reaches people through food, with kale and spinach among the richest sources and egg yolk another common one.[1] Supplements are commonly extracted from Mexican marigold petals, and a review describes microalgae as an alternative source under study.[1][15] A 2020 review notes that the body cannot make lutein itself and that lutein carries a Generally Regarded as Safe designation, with minimal side effects reported on long-term consumption.[12]

Supplement products are typically capsules or softgels combining lutein with zeaxanthin, sometimes alongside omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin E or zinc, and the AREDS2 formulation is sold in this form for people with AMD [21]. Eye-health products form the largest segment of the commercial lutein market, which also spans pet food, animal and fish feed and food colouring [1].

Observational studies had linked higher dietary lutein and zeaxanthin with lower AMD risk, and this motivated AREDS2 [16][22]. The first Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) enrolled 4,757 people aged 55 to 80 between 1992 and 1998; its formula of vitamins C and E, beta-carotene, zinc and copper reduced progression from intermediate to advanced AMD by about 25 percent [21].

AREDS2 was launched in 2006 to test whether adding lutein plus zeaxanthin or omega-3 fatty acids improved that formula, and whether beta-carotene could be dropped, since beta-carotene had been associated with higher lung cancer incidence in smokers and former smokers [21][17]. The resulting AREDS2 formula replaced beta-carotene with lutein (10 mg) and zeaxanthin (2 mg) [21].

Regulators have considered health claims for the pigments: according to Wikipedia, the US FDA rejected a qualified health claim in 2005 and the European Food Safety Authority rejected vision-related claims in 2014 [22].

Lutein and zeaxanthin are xanthophyll carotenoids and isomers the body can interconvert.[1] Both concentrate in the macula, where reviews attribute antioxidant and anti-inflammatory roles to them, although encyclopedic sources state the exact function is not fully established.[1][12]

AREDS2, published in JAMA in 2013, was a randomised trial in 4,203 people aged 50 to 85 at 82 clinical sites [16][21]. Adding lutein plus zeaxanthin or omega-3s to the AREDS formula had no added overall effect on advanced AMD, though the revised formula without beta-carotene performed comparably, and neither supplement changed the need for cataract surgery [21]. Former smokers who took beta-carotene had a higher incidence of lung cancer [21].

AREDS2 was a phase 3 trial in people with or at risk of age-related macular degeneration and cataract, enrolling 4,203 participants from 2006 [3]. Summaries report that the lutein and zeaxanthin formulation did not reduce AMD progression overall, with a possible reduction in people whose diets were low in these carotenoids, and no overall reduction in cataract surgery [1]. A 2023 Cochrane review is described as finding little effect on AMD progression versus placebo and insufficient evidence for early AMD [1].

The AREDS2 trial, published in JAMA in 2013, tested lutein plus zeaxanthin and omega-3 fatty acids as additions to the AREDS formulation of antioxidant vitamins and zinc; it was motivated by observational data suggesting that higher dietary lutein and zeaxanthin, omega-3 intake, or both might lower the risk of advanced AMD.[16] A long-term follow-up report, AREDS2 Report 28, examined 10-year outcomes after the beta carotene in the original formula was replaced by lutein and zeaxanthin, partly because beta carotene had been associated with higher lung cancer risk in people who smoked.[17]

A 2025 multicenter randomized trial reported that oral antioxidant and lutein/zeaxanthin supplements slowed progression of geographic atrophy toward the fovea in AMD.[18] Other randomized work covers children's dynamic visual and cognitive performance with lutein and zeaxanthin and working memory in older adults taking a combined omega-3, carotenoid and vitamin E supplement.[19][20]

Smaller registered trials have examined other outcomes, including visual function in healthy people (terminated, n=14) [4], vision in people with albinism (n=10) [5], supplementation in pregnancy (phase 2, n=47) [6], macular pigment density in people with and without wet AMD (n=200) [7], night vision (n=27) [8], dry eye (n=110) [9] and a phase 2/3 trial of carotenoid supplementation and normal ocular health [2], registered under retinal ageing (n=88) [10]. A planned trial in menopausal women is registered to examine cognition [11]. The registry entries describe designs and populations rather than results, and no registered trial listed here targets cosmetic eye appearance.

The only well-established effect of excessive intake is carotenodermia, a yellow-orange skin tint. Encyclopedic sources give an observed safe level of 20 mg/day and note that US and European authorities have not set an upper intake limit [1]. Lutein is approved as a food additive (E161b) in the EU and Australia and New Zealand; in the US it is permitted in supplements but not as a colouring for human foods [1].

Wikipedia reports that human studies found no adverse effects at 20 mg/day of zeaxanthin for up to six months, that the European Food Safety Authority has proposed an acceptable daily intake of 0.75 mg/kg body weight, and that as of 2016 neither the FDA nor EFSA had set a tolerable upper intake level [22]. The AREDS formulation containing beta-carotene is not recommended for current or former smokers, which is why the AREDS2 formula omitted it [21]. Lutein supplements are typically sold as dietary supplements, which are not approved by regulators for treating eye disease [1].

Lutein and zeaxanthin are discussed alongside other eye-health and skin-health nutrients, including omega-3 fatty acids, vitamin E and zinc in the AREDS2 formula [21], and alongside other carotenoid and polyphenol photoprotective supplements reviewed in 2025 [13]. Microalgae are under study as an alternative commercial source of lutein [15].

timeline.event: Enrolment begins in the first Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS); it runs to 1998 with 4,757 participants, and its formula later reduces progression to advanced AMD by about 25 percent [21].
The US FDA rejects a qualified health claim for lutein and zeaxanthin, according to Wikipedia [22].
AREDS2, a phase 3 trial of lutein and zeaxanthin among other nutrients, begins enrolment [3][21].
AREDS2 results are published in JAMA; lutein and zeaxanthin show no added overall benefit on AMD progression in the main analysis [16][21].
The European Food Safety Authority rejects vision-related health claims, according to Wikipedia [22].
AREDS2 Report 28 reports 10-year outcomes after beta-carotene is replaced with lutein/zeaxanthin [17].
A Cochrane review of 26 studies reports little effect of the supplements on AMD progression compared with placebo [1].

chain: Lutein and zeaxanthin are taken as oral supplements or eaten in greens and egg yolks
The pigments build up in the macula and circulate in tissues, including skin
Users aim for healthy eyes and a warmer, protected-looking complexion
angle.text: People take lutein and zeaxanthin as part of an eye-health and skin-care routine, aiming for healthy-looking eyes and a complexion protected from light exposure. The documented effect on appearance is the carotenoid skin tint at high intake; the eye outcomes studied are medical, such as macular pigment and AMD.
